opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it's one where the answer has shifted quite a bit over the last few years.

My background is really in simulation-heavy reinforcement learning, training legged robots in massively parallel simulators where you can run thousands of robots at once and collect years of experience in a few hours. For locomotion, that approach has worked remarkably well. You can train a policy entirely in simulation, with domain randomization over things like friction, masses, motor dynamics and terrain, and deploy it zero-shot on the real robot. For that class of problems, I'd argue you don't need much real data at all for the policy itself.

Where real data becomes really valuable, in my view, is in two places. The first is closing the gap on the things simulation models poorly. Actuator dynamics are a classic example. Some of the earliest successful sim-to-real work on legged robots trained an actuator network from real motor data and plugged it into the simulator. So real data doesn't train the policy directly. It makes the simulator more faithful. I think that's an underrated way of combining the two: use real data to improve the simulator, then let the simulator do the heavy lifting.

The second is perception and manipulation, where the gap is much larger. Simulating contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, or realistic camera images is still hard. There, real demonstrations, teleoperation data, and increasingly large pre-trained vision and language models bring something simulation can't easily provide: the richness and messiness of the real world.

So the picture I find most compelling is layered. Simulation is where you learn the physical, dynamic skills, the low-level control, balance, reacting to disturbances, because you need enormous amounts of trial and error that would be impractical or dangerous on hardware. Real-world data, and the priors from foundation models trained on internet-scale data, cover the semantic side: what to do, what objects are, how a scene is structured. Then you fine-tune or adapt on the real robot to absorb whatever residual mismatch remains.

I'd also push back a bit on the idea that it's one or the other. People sometimes frame it as "sim versus real," but the strongest systems I've seen treat simulation as a data generator that you keep calibrating against reality. The real data tells you where your simulator is lying to you, and the simulator gives you scale. If you get that loop right, you get the best of both.

r001.rationale: It reserves real data for simulator mismatches, such as actuator dynamics, and for perception and manipulation tasks that are difficult to simulate.

r002.rationale: It describes simulation doing substantial work and being calibrated against reality, but does not predict that simulators will cover an increasing share of training tasks as they improve.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what part of the robot you're training, because the two kinds of data have very different strengths.

Simulation is where you want to do the bulk of the learning, especially for anything involving locomotion or whole-body control. The reason is simple: you can run thousands of robots in parallel, you can reset them instantly, you can let them fall over ten million times without breaking anything, and you can randomize terrain, friction, mass, motor properties, all of it. That volume and that diversity is what makes reinforcement learning actually work. You simply cannot get that from hardware. If you tried to collect the equivalent experience on a real legged robot, you'd be replacing actuators every afternoon.

But simulation has a ceiling, which is the sim-to-real gap. Contacts are never quite right, actuator dynamics are approximated, and perception, especially depth cameras or anything vision-based, is where the gap is widest. So the question becomes: where do you spend your real-world data, which is expensive and scarce?

My view is that real data is most valuable for closing specific gaps rather than for learning the policy from scratch. A few examples. You can collect real actuator data and fit a small network that models the motor response, then put that model into the simulator, which is what we did with the ANYmal work. That's a tiny amount of real data that dramatically improves every simulated rollout. Similarly, you can use real sensor data to calibrate noise models or to train the perception stack, and then let the control policy learn in sim on top of that.

The other direction is also interesting, which is using real-world rollouts to fine-tune a policy that was pretrained in simulation. That's becoming more practical as the base policies get more robust, because the robot doesn't fall as often, so the data you collect is actually useful. But I'd be cautious about treating real-world fine-tuning as the main learning signal. It's slow, it's dangerous for the hardware, and if your sim is good enough, you often don't need it.

So if I had to summarize: learn behavior in simulation, use real data to make the simulation more honest, and reserve direct real-world learning for the residual that you genuinely can't model. And then push hard on making the simulator better, because every improvement there pays off across everything you train.

r001.rationale: The response says to use real data to close specific simulation gaps and reserve direct real-world learning for what cannot be modeled.

r002.rationale: It advocates improving simulators, but does not predict that simulators will cover an increasing share of robot-training tasks as they improve.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. Simulation gives you a way to collect a lot of experience cheaply and safely, especially for things like locomotion, where learning involves falling down many times. You can also vary the environment and the robot’s properties to make the policy more robust. But ultimately, the robot has to work in the real world, and simulation will always have limitations.

So I wouldn’t think of it as choosing a fixed ratio of real and simulated data. I’d use simulation to learn the broad behavior, then use real-world experience to understand where the simulation is wrong. That can help you improve the simulator, or it can be used to adapt the policy directly. The important thing is that it’s a loop: real-world results inform what you train in simulation, and then you test whether that training actually improves the robot.

r001.rationale: The response uses real-world experience to identify simulation errors and guide simulator improvement or policy adaptation, but it does not propose reserving real training data for specific cases where simulation is inadequate.

r002.rationale: It says simulation has limitations and should be improved through a real-world feedback loop, but does not predict that improving simulators will cover an increasing share of training tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. In simulation, you can collect a huge amount of experience in parallel, including failures that would be expensive or dangerous on a real robot. So it’s a great place to learn the basic behavior. But you shouldn’t expect the simulator to capture everything perfectly.

Real data can help you understand where those differences matter: the contact dynamics, the actuators, delays, things like that. You can use that information to improve the simulation and decide what to randomize during training. Then you bring the policy back to the robot and test whether it actually transfers.

So I see it as an iterative process, rather than choosing some fixed percentage of real and simulated data. Use simulation for scale, and use real experience to keep that training grounded in what the robot actually encounters.

r001.rationale: The response assigns real-robot experience to identifying and addressing simulator gaps, while using simulation for broad-scale training.

r002.rationale: It describes simulation as useful for scale but does not predict that simulators will cover a growing share of training tasks as they improve.
